lawyer:
Md Ramjan Ali Sikder for Dr Kamal Hossain Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General with AM Aminuddin, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Sew Bishar Prasad ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Abu Sayeed Ahammed J: This Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the petitioner Sew Bihari Parsed, sole proprietor of Messers Bangladesh Traders, having his business office at Sena Kallyan Bhaban, Room 0.901, 9th Floor, 195 Motijheel Commercial Area Dhaka, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 6-5-95 (Annexure-E) issued by the respondent No. 3 the Appraiser, Chittagong Customs House, Chittagong, directing the petitioner to submit the bill of entry declaring the value of imported goods namely, sugar, for fixing the rate of customs duty on the basis of indicative value and declaring the same arbitrarily for the purpose of assessment of the Customs duty, VAT and other charges on the consignment of the petitioner, in question.

2. The petitioner according to SRO No. 214- ATN/93/1527/Shulka dated 28-10-1993, wherein the value of the questioned Sugar was affixed at US$ 350 per metric ton, by opening LC No. D/C/94240 dated 18-8-1994 through American Express Bank, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, imported 10,500 metric tons of white crystal sugar. The SRO is Annexure-“A” and the L/C is Annexure “B”

3. After arrival of the goods, the clearing Agent of the petitioner submitted the bill of entry for releasing the goods' after assessment of customs duty at the aforesaid rate of the value as shown in the papers and documents of the petitioner importer. But the respondent No. 3 by his order dated 6-5-95 directed the petitioner to submit bill of entry declaring the value of the imported goods at the rate of US$ 401.55 calling it indicative value instead of declared value which was at the rate of US$ 350 per metric ton.

4. Bring aggrieved by that order (Annexure-C the petitioner has obtained the present Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution.

5. The Customs Authority has not filed affidavit-in-opposition and its case is that under section 25(1) of the Customs Act, the indicative value can be assessed and accordingly, the impugned order has been issued upon the petitioner asking him to value his goods accordingly and to pay customs duty upon that value which the customs authority call indicative value.

6. In this case, the tax has been imposed on the basis of the term 'indicative value' but this term indicative value is not found anywhere within the four comers of the Customs Act, 1969 and, as such, it is submitted for the petitioner that the impugned order is illegal and it has infringed the fundamental right of the petitioner.

<u>7. Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder, the learned Counsel for the petitioner in support of his argument cites the decision in the case of Russell Vegetable Oil Ltd vs Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others, reported in 5 MLR (HC) 121=52 DLR 382. In the said decision, in para 13 while opinion as to standard in fixation of value, their Lordships have held, as under:</u>

<u>"The price as mentioned in the letter of credit and the commercial invoice prima facie shows that the price mentioned in those documents is the market value between the seller and the buyer, in other words, the supplier and the consignee. Therefore, as per provision of section 25(1) said invoice price is to be taken to be the normal price unless of course, the Customs Authority have no arbitrary right to reject the invoice value. If they do not accept the invoice value they must have sufficient materials to support their action. There is no such material whatsoever which tends to show that the consignment in question has been under invoiced."</u>

<u>Section 25(1) also has proved that the value of any imported goods shall be fixed according to normal value of the Articles i.e. the price which they would fetch, on the date as referred to in section 30 on sale of the goods in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other.</u>

8. So we are of the opinion that the section 25(1) of Customs Act also recognise and accept the view that the price of the imparted goods should be affixed at the normal value vis-a-vis the market value. So nowhere, there is indicative value which has been accepted as the basis for imposition of customs duty in this particular case and the customs authority enhanced the value of the goods from US$ 305 per metric ton to US$ 401 per metric tons to the great prejudice of the petitioner.

<u>9. In another unreported decision of the High Court Division in which a bunch of cases have been decided their Lordships nave held as under:</u>

<u>"We are of the view that the age old methods determining the normal price with various adjectives i.e. indicative value, enhanced valuation price, recorded value, loaded value, Commissioner's value, etc have no sanction in law and, as such, we direct the respondents not to use such attributes or any other adjective so far the normal value is concerned. The name of parties in the bunch of cases are Md Ayub and others vs Collector of Customs and others in Writ Petition Nos.1495 of 1996 and others.</u>

<u>10. In another decision reported in 4 BLC 85 relevant page 99 in para 62 [Rahmania Vanaspati Product Ltd vs Collector of Customs], their Lordships have held as follows:</u>

<u>"From a reading of the provision of sections 25(1), (2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Act it is very much seen that if customs authority is authorised to assess customs duties on imported merchandise at the value prevalent on the date the Bill of entry is presented for assessment of customs duties. The undenied position is that the customs authority fixed the "indicative value" for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO and CPO, the kind of merchandises imported by the petitioners, much long before the presentation of the Bill of Entry, This being the factual position, the 'indicative value' that has been fixed by the circular dated 3-6-1994 cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of section 25(1), (2) (3) and section 30(1) of the Act."</u>

<u>Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder, the learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that in this case, affixing value on the basis calling it indicative value, the customs authority has committed illegality against the vested legal right of the petitioner, because his goods are to be valued at the rate of normal value as per provisions of section 25(1) of the Customs Act.</u>

<u>11. We find force in this submission, because, we do not get anywhere the term. indicative value, which can be made the basis or standard legally for fixing the value of the imported goods for the purpose of imposing customs duty, rather, in the aforesaid decisions the same has been made nugatory.</u>

12. Our meticulous reading of the provision of Section 25(1) as a whole also does not approve the said term, namely, indicative value which is a mere dreaming one without any basis. The decision of the High Court Division although have no binding force upon us, but those have got persuasive value. So, we accept the opinions contributed by those decisions.

13. Mr Aminuddin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent, in view of the impugned order passed vide Annexure-'F", submits that the petitioner avoiding to appear before the customs authority, has come up with this writ petition. So it is not maintainable.

14. We see that by the impugned order, the Customs authority did not, in fact, direct the petitioner to appear before the customs authority and to show cause, as to the grievance of the petitioner, rather, after fixing up the mind of the custom authority, illegally and arbitrarily, they have directed the petitioner to appear before them only for the purpose of converting the value of the goods to facilitate the customs authority to impose higher duty and tax. On hearing the submissions of both parties it led us to find that the customs authority should fix the value of the goods according to normal price which could be found from the bill of entry, to be considered along with the invoice value submitted by the by petitioner as to the consignment in question.

15. For the reasons and discussions made above, we find merits in this Rule. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The fixation of valuation and imposition of taxes by the impugned order is declared to have been made without lawful authority and ultra vires of the Constitution and are of no legal effect. The Customs authority, therefore, is directed to affix the value of the goods in question under section 25(1) of the Customs Act according to the normal value of the goods which is also called market value as incorporated in the bill of entry and the invoice.

The Commissioner of Customs is directed to release the bank guarantees furnished by the petitioner in terms of the Rule within 15 days from the date of receipt of this order.

No costs.

End.
